at.out: Tuple and domain relational calculus and Codd's completeness theorem are formal-semantics theory with no direct operational payoff for a data-engineering course; the topic teaches the algebra operationally instead.

items.item: Aggregation depends on bag multiplicities: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(column) counts non-null values, and SUM needs every row counted once, which is why collapsing duplicates before an aggregate silently changes the answer
Operator precedence and associativity among the set operators (INTERSECT tighter than UNION/EXCEPT; UNION/EXCEPT left-to-right) changes what an unparenthesized multi-operator query actually means

items.item: Real engines route UNION ALL, UNION, and INTERSECT/EXCEPT through three distinct execution paths (Append only; Append plus Agg/Sort; a dedicated SetOp node), so defaulting to the cheapest form that is still correct is a real, measurable choice

resolved: Confirmed EXCEPT (without ALL) can drop to zero rows even where EXCEPT ALL keeps one, not merely 'fewer rows'; added as its own worked case rather than assumed
Confirmed the extra UNION pass is paid even when the two branches are known to be disjoint, since the planner cannot know that without doing the work
Checked every pushdown and dedup number against examples.py rather than restating the draft's prose numbers
